result:
A connection pool keeps a set of already-open database connections alive and lends them out to your code, instead of opening a new one for every query. When a request needs the database it borrows an idle connection, runs its queries, and returns it to the pool rather than closing it; if none are idle, the pool opens another up to a configured maximum, and beyond that callers wait in a queue until one is returned or a timeout fires.

It helps because opening a connection is expensive: a TCP handshake, usually TLS, authentication, and on the server side allocating session memory or (in Postgres) forking a whole process. That can cost several milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, often more than the query itself, so reusing connections removes that overhead from every request.

The cap matters as much as the reuse. Databases degrade badly with too many concurrent connections, since each one holds memory and competes for CPU and locks, so the pool acts as a throttle that turns a traffic spike into brief queuing in your app instead of an overloaded database.

The practical things to get right are the pool size (smaller than most people expect; a few times the database's core count is a common starting point, and remember the total is pool size times the number of app instances), always returning connections (a leaked connection eventually starves the pool), and letting the pool validate or recycle connections so it does not hand out ones that the server or a firewall has silently dropped.
